questions.q: Physically, what does it mean to 'apply the Hadamard gate' to a real qubit?
options: Letting the qubit evolve under a specifically engineered Hamiltonian for a specifically calibrated duration, such that the resulting U(t) equals the Hadamard matrix
Flipping a physical classical switch connected to the qubit
Measuring the qubit twice in quick succession
Applying an arbitrary non-unitary transformation chosen by the circuit designer
questions.explain: A gate is not a separate mechanism from physics -- it IS Schrödinger-equation time evolution under a chosen Hamiltonian for a chosen duration, engineered so U(t) comes out equal to the desired gate matrix.

questions.q: What do the verified facts H·H=I, X·X=I, and S²=Z have in common?
options: They are all concrete confirmations that specific real gates are unitary and behave consistently with being physical time-evolution operators
They show that Hadamard, Pauli-X, and the S gate are actually the same gate
They prove that quantum gates are not unitary after all
They only apply to classical logic gates, not quantum ones
questions.explain: Each identity was independently verified by direct matrix/complex-number computation, and each demonstrates self-consistent unitary behavior (e.g. H and X being self-inverse, S squaring to Z) -- concrete evidence that real gates satisfy the unitarity this chapter derives from physics.

questions.q: Why can a non-unitary matrix never correspond to a valid stretch of Schrödinger-equation time evolution?
options: Because unitarity (U†U=I) is exactly the condition that keeps a state's total measurement probability equal to 1 at every moment -- a non-unitary operator would mean probability isn't conserved, which is physically impossible for a closed system
Because non-unitary matrices are mathematically undefined
Because non-unitary matrices can only be applied to classical bits, never qubits
There is no real restriction; any matrix can represent valid time evolution
questions.explain: U†U=I guarantees ⟨ψ(t)|ψ(t)⟩ stays at 1 for all t. A non-unitary operator would let total probability drift away from 1, which isn't a design flaw -- it's a mathematical impossibility for evolution governed by the Schrödinger equation.

questions.q: Why are quantum gates described as reversible, in contrast to classical AND/OR gates?
options: Every unitary matrix has an inverse (its conjugate transpose), so the input to any quantum gate can always be recovered exactly from its output -- classical AND/OR gates destroy information and generally cannot be undone this way
Classical AND and OR gates are also fully reversible, just like quantum gates
Quantum gates are reversible only when they happen to be the identity matrix
Reversibility has nothing to do with whether a gate is unitary
questions.explain: Because U†U=I for any unitary U, the inverse operation U† always exists and recovers the original input exactly. Classical gates like AND lose information (you can't always tell which inputs produced a given output), so they are generally not reversible.

questions.q: In a quantum circuit, where does information actually get irreversibly discarded, if gates themselves never lose information?
options: At measurement -- a fundamentally different kind of step from gate application, which is probabilistic and collapses the state rather than evolving it unitarily
Information is never discarded anywhere in a quantum circuit, including at measurement
Information is discarded at every gate application, just like in classical circuits
Information is discarded only when a circuit uses the Hadamard gate specifically
questions.explain: Gates are unitary and therefore reversible/information-preserving; measurement (Chapter 3) is the genuinely different, probabilistic, state-collapsing step where information about the superposition is lost -- not something that happens during ordinary gate application.
